[[securing_repositories]]
= Securing Repositories

Every JAR, POM, and plugin your project uses is fetched from a repository, and every repository you declare is an implicit statement of trust.
If an attacker can influence what a repository serves, or trick your build into asking a repository it shouldn't, they can inject arbitrary code into your build.

This page covers two practices that protect the repository layer:

1. *Use trusted repositories:* declare only repositories you control or explicitly vet, over HTTPS, in one central place.
2. *Filter repository content:* restrict which coordinates each repository is allowed to serve, and route sensitive artifacts to exclusive sources.

image::securing-builds/securing-builds-2.png[]

[[sec:trusted_repositories]]
== Use Trusted Repositories

A trusted repository is one whose contents you can vouch for.
That trust usually comes from one of three places:

1. You run the repository yourself (an internal Artifactory, Nexus, or similar).
2. The repository is operated by an organization with a strong integrity record (for example, Maven Central).
3. The repository serves artifacts you have already verified out-of-band, typically through checksums or signatures recorded in your build.

Every other repository is untrusted by default, even if it appears to work.
An untrusted repository can serve a legitimate artifact today and a compromised one tomorrow; your build has no way to tell the difference unless verification is in place.

[[sec:centralize_repository_declarations]]
=== Centralize Repository Declarations

Repositories declared inside individual subprojects are hard to audit.
A reviewer looking at `settings.gradle.kts` cannot tell whether a subproject three levels deep has silently added a repository that the rest of the build knows nothing about.

Since Gradle 6.8, `dependencyResolutionManagement` in `settings.gradle(.kts)` provides a central place to declare project repositories (see <<centralizing_repositories.adoc#centralized-repository-declaration,Centralizing Repository Declarations>> for the full reference):

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-centralized/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=centralized]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-centralized/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=centralized]"]
====

`repositoriesMode` has three values:

[cols="1,3"]
|===
|Mode |Behavior

|`PREFER_PROJECT` (default)
|Any repository declared in a subproject's `build.gradle(.kts)` overrides the repositories declared in settings. Convenient, but subproject declarations bypass central control.

|`PREFER_SETTINGS`
|Repositories declared in subprojects are ignored, and Gradle logs a warning for each. The settings repositories always win.

|`FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS`
|Any repository declaration in a subproject causes the build to fail. Nothing outside `settings.gradle(.kts)` can add a repository.
|===

For security-sensitive builds, use `FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS`.
It guarantees that the only repositories your build will ever contact are the ones listed in `settings.gradle(.kts)`, where they are visible to every reviewer and every audit.

WARNING: The default is `PREFER_PROJECT`. Setting `dependencyResolutionManagement.repositories { ... }` without also setting `repositoriesMode` still lets subprojects override the central list. Set the mode explicitly.

Plugin repositories follow a separate rule.
Declare them once in `settings.gradle(.kts)` under `pluginManagement`:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-pluginManagement/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=plugin-management]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-pluginManagement/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=plugin-management]"]
====

NOTE: `pluginManagement` does not have a `repositoriesMode` equivalent. Plugin repositories are always resolved from `settings.gradle(.kts)`, so the concern that motivates `FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS` does not apply, no subproject can add a plugin repository.

[[sec:prefer_internal_mirrors]]
=== Prefer an Internal Mirror

Consuming public repositories directly means your build depends on the availability and integrity of an upstream service you do not control.
An internal mirror sits between your build and the public internet and gives you three properties that a direct dependency on Maven Central cannot:

1. *Auditability:* every artifact your build has ever downloaded is recorded in one place you own.
2. *Reproducibility:* artifacts remain available even if they are yanked or deleted upstream.
3. *Containment:* you can block or quarantine a compromised artifact for every project at once, without touching every build file in the organization.

A mirror doesn't remove trust from the equation.
It relocates it.
Whatever you used to trust in the upstream now lives in the mirror, and any weakness in how you run the mirror becomes a weakness in every build that depends on it.
Before adopting one:

* *Serve the mirror over HTTPS*. An HTTP-only mirror is a downgrade, not an upgrade, over talking to Maven Central directly.
* *Verify artifacts on ingest.* When the mirror pulls an artifact from an upstream repository for the first time, check the artifact against the upstream's published checksum (or signature) before it becomes available to downstream builds. Otherwise, the mirror will faithfully cache a compromised artifact and serve it to every project.
* *Do not skip dependency verification because "it's internal."* `verification-metadata.xml` should cover artifacts served from the mirror the same way it covers anything else. The mirror is a distribution mechanism, not a trust decision.
* *Restrict who can publish to the mirror.* The mirror's write ACL determines who can inject artifacts into every build in the organization. Treat it as production infrastructure.

There are three ways to point Gradle at a mirror, in order of preference.

[[sec:mirror_via_settings]]
==== 1. Declare the Mirror in `settings.gradle(.kts)`

The direct approach. Every build in the repository sees the mirror; nothing else can add a public repository if `FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS` is set:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-mirror/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=mirror]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-mirror/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=mirror]"]
====

This is the pattern to prefer for any repository you control.
The routing decision lives in `settings.gradle(.kts)` where every reviewer sees it, and content filtering applies to the mirror the same way it applies to any other repository.

[[sec:mirror_via_init_script]]
==== 2. Redirect Existing Builds via an Init Script

When you cannot or don't want to modify every project's `settings.gradle(.kts)`, for example, because you're rolling out a mirror across an organization with many existing repositories, an init script in `~/.gradle/init.d/` can rewrite repositories at initialization time.

[source,kotlin]
.~/.gradle/init.d/mirror.init.gradle.kts
----
val mirrorUrl = "https://repo.internal.acme.com/maven-public"

settingsEvaluated {
    pluginManagement.repositories {
        clear()
        maven {
            name = "internalMirror"
            url = uri(mirrorUrl)
        }
    }
    dependencyResolutionManagement.repositories {
        clear()
        maven {
            name = "internalMirror"
            url = uri(mirrorUrl)
        }
    }
}

allprojects {
    repositories {
        // Replace project-declared repositories with the mirror
        val allRepos = toList()
        clear()
        allRepos.forEach { repo ->
            if (repo is MavenArtifactRepository) {
                maven {
                    name = repo.name
                    url = uri(mirrorUrl)
                }
            } else {
                add(repo)
            }
        }
    }
}
----

This pattern has security costs:

* *The init script is an implicit trust anchor.* Every build on a machine that has this file runs it, see the guidance on init script trust in <<securing_build_tool.adoc#sec:init_scripts,Securing the Build Tool>>.
Deploy the init script through your existing configuration management, not by asking developers to `curl` it into `~/.gradle/init.d`.
* *The script silently overrides what build scripts declare.* A developer reading `build.gradle.kts` will not see the mirror; a Build Scan will.
Communicate the rewrite clearly, or expect confusion when local behavior diverges from CI.

Prefer this pattern only when option 1 is not feasible, and revisit whenever you can move projects to explicit settings-level declarations.

[[sec:mirror_via_maven_settings]]
==== 3. Reuse Maven `settings.xml` Mirrors

Organizations already invested in Maven often maintain their mirror configuration in `~/.m2/settings.xml`.
Since 8.13, Gradle can read those same mirrors instead of requiring the configuration to be duplicated (see <<centralizing_repositories.adoc#sec:reusing-maven-mirror-settings,Reusing mirror settings from Maven>> for the full behavior, including `mirrorOf` matching rules and unsupported features):

[source,properties]
.gradle.properties
----
org.gradle.mirror.maven.settings=true
----

WARNING: This is an incubating feature and is disabled by default.

With the property set, Gradle reads mirrors from the user and global `settings.xml`, matches each declared Maven repository against them using Maven's `mirrorOf` grammar, and resolves from the mirror instead.
Credentials come from the `<server>` entry whose id matches the *mirror* id.

This is the right choice only if you already have a working Maven mirror setup and want Gradle to honor the same routing.
It is not a general-purpose redirection mechanism, and it applies to Maven repositories only.
S3, GCS, local file, and Ivy repositories pass through unchanged.

Two properties matter for the security posture of a `settings.xml`-driven setup:

* *`settings.xml` becomes part of your trust chain.* Anyone who can write to `~/.m2/settings.xml` can silently redirect every Gradle build on the machine.
Treat the file with the same care as `~/.gradle/gradle.properties`.
* *Publishing is not affected.* Mirrors apply to resolution only. Publishing always uploads to the URL declared in the build.
This is the safe default, since you want publishes to hit the real destination, not the mirror. Confirm it anyway when auditing the flow.

[[sec:require_https]]
=== Require HTTPS

Since Gradle 7, plaintext HTTP repositories are rejected by default.
When Gradle encounters a repository whose URL is not HTTPS (or an equivalent secure scheme), it throws `InsecureProtocolException` and refuses to resolve dependencies from it.

The relevant flag is `allowInsecureProtocol` on any `MavenArtifactRepository` or `IvyArtifactRepository`.
Its default is `false`.

.settings.gradle.kts (do NOT do this)
====
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-insecure/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=insecure]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-insecure/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=insecure]"]
====

Setting `isAllowInsecureProtocol = true` is a security downgrade, anyone on the network path between your build and the repository can intercept the artifacts you download and substitute their own.
Use HTTPS.

If a legacy internal repository is HTTP-only, put a TLS-terminating proxy in front of it and update `distributionUrl` to the HTTPS endpoint.
Enabling `allowInsecureProtocol` is not a solution; it is a permanent widening of your attack surface.

[[sec:avoid_dynamic_versions_at_repos]]
=== Avoid Dynamic Versions

Two patterns weaken repository trust even when the repository itself is legitimate:

* *Dynamic versions* (`1.+`, `latest.release`) let the repository decide what your build compiles against.
A malicious or mistaken publish upstream reaches your build on the next resolution. Pin to exact versions.
* *Anonymous repositories that require credentials* accept whatever the network delivers. Always use HTTPS.
If a repository requires credentials, provide them through Gradle credentials, not by embedding them in build scripts.

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-credentials/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=credentials]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-credentials/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=credentials]"]
====

With this declaration, Gradle reads the credentials from `gradle.properties` (or Gradle-managed credential storage) as `internalUsername` and `internalPassword`, matching the repository's `name`.
No secrets appear in the build script.

Three credential types are supported on `AuthenticationSupported` repositories:

1. `PasswordCredentials`: reads `<repoName>Username` / `<repoName>Password`.
2. `HttpHeaderCredentials`: reads `<repoName>AuthHeaderName` / `<repoName>AuthHeaderValue`. Useful for repositories that authenticate via a header (for example, a bearer token).
3. `AwsCredentials`: reads `<repoName>AccessKey` / `<repoName>SecretKey` / `<repoName>SessionToken`. Useful for S3-backed Maven repositories.

[[sec:metadata_sources]]
=== Configure `metadataSources` Deliberately

A repository declaration exposes a `metadataSources` block that controls how Gradle resolves module metadata:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-metadataSources/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=metadata-sources]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-metadataSources/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=metadata-sources]"]
====

The important security lever here is the `artifact()` source:

* `mavenPom()` / `ivyDescriptor()` / `gradleMetadata()` all require a metadata descriptor that pins the artifact to its coordinates, its dependencies, and (with Gradle Module Metadata) additional integrity data.
* `artifact()` tells Gradle it may resolve a coordinate by asking the repository whether a matching file exists, with no metadata descriptor.
There is no POM, no `.module`, and no validation that the file at that path is actually the artifact those coordinates describe.

Do not enable `artifact()` on repositories that host third-party or public content.
Reserve it for tightly controlled internal locations where you accept the risk of coordinate-only resolution.

[[sec:content_filtering]]
== Filter Repository Content

By default, when a build resolves a dependency, Gradle asks every declared repository in order until one answers.
That default is convenient but it has two security consequences worth understanding.

First, every repository you declare sees the full list of coordinates your build asks for.
If you declare a public repository alongside a private one, the public repository learns the names of your private artifacts every time it is queried.
This is called *dependency name leakage,* and it is a real vector for *dependency confusion* attacks.
An attacker who knows the name of your internal `com.acme.secret-tool` package can publish a package of the same name to a public repository and wait for a misconfigured build to pick it up.

Second, an artifact you expected to come from a trusted repository can silently come from a less trusted one if the trusted repository is briefly unavailable or if resolution order changes.

Content filtering solves both problems by declaring, up front, which coordinates each repository is allowed to serve.
See <<filtering_repository_content.adoc#repository-content-filtering,Filtering Repository Content>> for the full reference including Maven-repository-specific filters and Ivy dynamic resolve mode.

[[sec:content_filtering_basics]]
=== Restrict Groups to Repositories

Every `ArtifactRepository` exposes a `content { ... }` block.
Inside that block you declare which groups, modules, versions, or configurations the repository is allowed to serve.
Filters apply *before* Gradle contacts the repository, so the repository never sees requests for coordinates it isn't allowed to serve.

The available filters are:

[cols="2,3"]
|===
|Filter |Effect

|`includeGroup(String)` / `excludeGroup(String)`
|Match a single exact group.

|`includeGroupByRegex(String)` / `excludeGroupByRegex(String)`
|Match groups by regular expression.

|`includeGroupAndSubgroups(String)` / `excludeGroupAndSubgroups(String)`
|Match a group and its dot-delimited subgroups. `com.acme` matches `com.acme`, `com.acme.foo`, and `com.acme.foo.bar`, but *not* `com.acmefoo`. Introduced in Gradle 8.1.

|`includeModule(String, String)` / `excludeModule(String, String)`
|Match `group:name` pairs.

|`includeModuleByRegex(String, String)` / `excludeModuleByRegex(String, String)`
|Match `group:name` by regular expression.

|`includeVersion(String, String, String)` / `excludeVersion(String, String, String)`
|Match a specific `group:name:version`.

|`includeVersionByRegex(String, String, String)` / `excludeVersionByRegex(String, String, String)`
|Match `group:name:version` by regular expression.

|`onlyForConfigurations(String...)` / `notForConfigurations(String...)`
|Restrict which configurations can resolve from this repository.
|===

A typical routing configuration:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-contentFilter/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=content-filter]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-contentFilter/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=content-filter]"]
====

With this configuration:

* Any request for a `com.acme*` artifact is sent *only* to the internal repository.
* Any request for anything else is sent *only* to Maven Central.
* Neither repository is ever asked about coordinates it isn't allowed to serve, so neither repository can learn the names of coordinates it shouldn't see.

TIP: Prefer `includeGroupAndSubgroups` and `excludeGroupAndSubgroups` over `includeGroup` / `excludeGroup` when your organization owns a group and its subgroups (e.g. `com.acme`, `com.acme.web`, `com.acme.mobile`). Filtering by exact group only would leave subgroups uncovered.

[[sec:content_filtering_exclusive]]
=== Make a Repository Exclusive for a Set of Coordinates

When an artifact must come from one specific repository and nowhere else, declare that repository as exclusive for those coordinates using link:{javadocPath}/org/gradle/api/artifacts/repositories/ExclusiveContentRepository.html[`ExclusiveContentRepository`]:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-exclusiveContent/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=exclusive-content]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/securing-builds/dependencyResolutionManagement-exclusiveContent/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=exclusive-content]"]
====

`exclusiveContent` is stronger than a plain include filter:

* Coordinates matched by the filter are resolved *only* from the exclusive repository.
* No other repository (even one that would normally match the same coordinates) is ever asked.
* The `filter { }` block accepts only *inclusive* rules (`includeGroup`, `includeGroupAndSubgroups`, `includeModule`, etc.). Exclusions are implicit: everything not included is excluded.

Use `exclusiveContent` for internal artifacts, mirrors that host a specific project, or any coordinate that must never be sourced from a public mirror under any circumstances.

[NOTE]
====
If you use `exclusiveContent` inside `pluginManagement`, it becomes illegal to add more repositories through project-level `buildscript.repositories`; the build will fail at configuration time.
Either declare all plugin repositories in settings or use non-exclusive content filters.
====

[[security_gradle]]
= Securing Gradle Builds

Every Gradle build pulls in code from external repositories, executes tools you didn't author, and publishes artifacts that others will trust.
Each step is a potential attack surface.

For a typical Gradle build, the supply chain has three layers:

1. *Repositories:* where artifacts are stored and served.
2. *Dependencies:* the libraries and plugins your project consumes.
3. *Build Tool:* Gradle itself, including the Wrapper, init scripts, and everything under `~/.gradle`.

Attacks can originate at any layer and then propagate downstream through published artifacts, transitive dependencies, or compromised tools.
Even the build tool itself is an attack vector.

image::securing-builds/securing-builds-1.png[]

Gradle provides features to protect each layer:

[cols="1,3,3"]
|===
|Layer |Common issues and attacks |How to protect it

|*Repositories*
a|
* Dependency-confusion attacks against private coordinates
* Leaking private package names to public mirrors
* Artifacts from unauthenticated or plaintext-HTTP repositories
a|
Centralize repository declarations, require HTTPS, restrict which coordinates each repository is allowed to serve, and mark internal artifacts as exclusive to internal repositories.

See <<securing_repositories.adoc#securing_repositories,Securing Repositories>>.

|*Dependencies*
a|
* Typosquatting and name-squatting
* Compromised or replaced artifacts
* Silent version drift from dynamic versions
* Publicly disclosed vulnerabilities in code the author intentionally published
a|
Screen for known vulnerabilities, verify artifact checksums to protect integrity, and verify PGP signatures to protect provenance.

See <<securing_dependencies.adoc#securing_dependencies,Securing Dependencies>>.

|*Build Tool*
a|
* Tampered Wrapper JAR or distribution
* Compromised init scripts under `~/.gradle/init.d`
* Compromised `buildSrc` or included builds
* Poisoned local or remote caches
* Credentials leaked through plain-text `gradle.properties` or the configuration cache
a|
Pin and verify the Gradle Wrapper and distribution, protect the Gradle User Home, guard init scripts and `buildSrc`, protect caches and the daemon, and stay on a supported Gradle release.

See <<securing_build_tool.adoc#securing_build_tool,Securing the Build Tool>>.
|===

[[composite_builds]]
= Composite Builds (Included Builds)
:keywords: composite build, included build

A composite build is a build that includes other builds; those builds are known as included builds.

[[composite_build_intro]]
A composite build is similar to a Gradle <<multi_project_builds.adoc#multi_project_builds,multi-project build>>, except that instead of including `subprojects`, entire `builds` are included.

This is done either <<#settings_defined_composite,using the Settings file>> and adding a build using `includeBuild()`:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=inc]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=inc]"]
====

Or <<#command_line_composite,using the CLI flag>> `--include-build`:

[source,bash]
----
$ ./gradlew build --include-build my-utils
----

[[composite_build_use_cases]]
== When to Use Composite Builds

Composite builds are useful in three broad scenarios:

1. **Developing libraries and consumers together**: If you maintain a library that another project depends on, composite builds let you work across both at the same time without publishing the library first. +
Gradle automatically substitutes the external dependency with a local source, so changes to the library are immediately visible in the consuming project.

2. **Organizing large codebases**: Composite builds let you split a large codebase into independent builds that can each be opened and worked on in isolation (for example, in the IDE), while still being buildable together as a whole. +
This is a common approach in monorepo setups.

3. **Sharing build logic**: Composite builds are the <<best_practices_structuring_builds.adoc#favor_composite_builds,recommended way>> to structure and share custom build logic across projects. +
<<sharing_build_logic_between_subprojects.adoc#sec:using_buildsrc,`buildSrc`>> is _essentially_ an included build that Gradle manages automatically; a <<sharing_build_logic_between_subprojects.adoc#sec:sharing_logic_via_composite_build,`build-logic`>> build included via `includeBuild()` in your settings file is the same idea, made explicit.

[[defining_composite_builds]]
== Composite Build Layout

Included builds do not share any configuration with other included builds.

IMPORTANT: Each included build is *configured* in isolation — included builds do not share repositories, plugins, or properties with one another or with the root build, but they can be *executed* together and depend on each other's tasks.

Composite builds typically take one of two layouts depending on the use case: a <<#codev_composite,*co-development* layout>>, where an included build lives outside the consumer and is substituted temporarily during development; or a <<#separate_composite,*monorepo* layout>>, where an uber-root build knits together a set of independent builds that can also be worked on in isolation.

NOTE: For reference, a *build tree* consists of the root build and all of its included builds, recursively.

[[codev_composite]]
=== Co-development Layout Example

The following example demonstrates *co-development* — temporarily substituting a dependency to work across a library and its consumer simultaneously.
You simply include the library directly into the consumer build:

[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, kotlin]
----
my-app/                             // The consumer build (your working directory)
├── settings.gradle.kts             // includeBuild("../my-utils")
├── build.gradle.kts
└── app/
    ├── build.gradle.kts            // Declares dependencies on 'number-utils' and 'string-utils'
    └── src/main/java/...

my-utils/                           // The library build (Included Build)
├── settings.gradle.kts             // Defines 'number-utils' and 'string-utils' subprojects
├── number-utils/
│   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   └── src/main/java/...
└── string-utils/
    ├── build.gradle.kts
    └── src/main/java/...
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, groovy]
----
my-app/                             // The consumer build (your working directory)
├── settings.gradle                 // includeBuild("../my-utils")
├── build.gradle
└── app/
    ├── build.gradle                // Declares dependencies on 'number-utils' and 'string-utils'
    └── src/main/java/...

my-utils/                           // The library build (Included Build)
├── settings.gradle                 // Defines 'number-utils' and 'string-utils' subprojects
├── number-utils/
│   ├── build.gradle
│   └── src/main/java/...
└── string-utils/
    ├── build.gradle
    └── src/main/java/...
----
=====

In this example, `my-utils` lives outside of `my-app` and is included temporarily during development. Once the library changes are published, the `includeBuild` can be removed.

The `my-app` root settings file looks as follows:

====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,kotlin]
.settings.gradle.kts
----
rootProject.name = "my-app"

include("app")
includeBuild("../my-utils")
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,groovy]
.settings.gradle
----
rootProject.name = "my-app"

include("app")
includeBuild("../my-utils")
----
=====
====

[[separate_composite]]
=== Monorepo Layout Example

The following example demonstrates a *monorepo* layout in which an uber-root build knits together independent builds.

[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, kotlin]
----
my-composite/                       // The root of the Composite Build
├── settings.gradle.kts
├── my-app/                         // The application build (Included Build #1)
│   ├── settings.gradle.kts
│   └── app/
│       ├── build.gradle.kts        // Declares dependencies on 'number-utils' and 'string-utils'
│       └── src/main/java/...
└── my-utils/                       // The utility library build (Included Build #2)
    ├── settings.gradle.kts         // Defines 'number-utils' and 'string-utils' subprojects
    ├── number-utils/
    │   ├── build.gradle.kts
    │   └── src/main/java/...
    └── string-utils/
        ├── build.gradle.kts
        └── src/main/java/...
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, groovy]
----
my-composite/                       // The root of the Composite Build
├── settings.gradle
├── my-app/                         // The application build (Included Build #1)
│   ├── settings.gradle
│   └── app/
│       ├── build.gradle            // Declares dependencies on 'number-utils' and 'string-utils'
│       └── src/main/java/...
└── my-utils/                       // The utility library build (Included Build #2)
    ├── settings.gradle             // Defines 'number-utils' and 'string-utils' subprojects
    ├── number-utils
    │   ├── build.gradle
    │   └── src/main/java/...
    └── string-utils
        ├── build.gradle
        └── src/main/java/...
----
=====

In this example, `my-composite` is a composite build that includes the `my-app` build and the `my-utils` build.
`my-app` and `my-utils` are included builds:

The `my-composite` root settings file looks as follows:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/groovy",files="settings.gradle[]"]
====

[[settings_defined_composite]]
== Defining a Composite Build via the Settings file

The settings file, `settings.gradle(.kts)`, can be used to add subprojects and included builds simultaneously using link:{groovyDslPath}/org.gradle.api.initialization.Settings.html#org.gradle.api.initialization.Settings:includeBuild(java.lang.Object)[Settings.includeBuild(java.lang.Object)].

Included builds are added by location using a file path:

* **Relative paths** are resolved relative to the directory containing the settings file - `includeBuild("../my-utils")`
* **Absolute paths** can also be used but are heavily discouraged - `includeBuild("/Users/user/projects/my-utils")`

The path should point to the **root directory** of the build (the directory containing the `settings.gradle(.kts)` file of the included build):

====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,kotlin]
.settings.gradle.kts
----
includeBuild("../dir/other-build")
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,groovy]
.settings.gradle
----
includeBuild("../dir/other-build")
----
=====
====

[[command_line_composite]]
== Defining a Composite Build via `--include-build`

The `--include-build` command-line argument turns the executed build into a composite, substituting dependencies from the included build into the executed build:

[source,bash]
----
$ ./gradlew --include-build ../my-utils run
----
[source,text]
----
include::{snippetsPath}/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/tests/basicCli.out[]
----

[[interacting_with_composite_builds]]
== Interacting with a Composite Build

Interacting with a composite build is generally similar to a regular multi-project build.
Tasks can be executed, tests can be run, and builds can be imported into the IDE.

[[composite_build_executing_tasks]]
=== Executing Tasks

Tasks from an included build can be executed from the command-line or IDE in the same way as tasks from a regular multi-project build.
Executing a task will result in task dependencies being executed, as well as those tasks required to build dependency artifacts from other included builds.

You can call a task in an included build using a fully qualified path, for example, `:included-build-name:project-name:taskName`:

[source,bash]
----
$ ./gradlew :included-build:subproject-a:compileJava
----
[source,text]
----
> Task :included-build:subproject-a:compileJava
----

Build, project, and task names can all be <<command_line_interface.adoc#sec:name_abbreviation,abbreviated>>:

[source,bash]
----
$ ./gradlew :i-b:sA:cJ
----
[source,text]
----
> Task :included-build:subproject-a:compileJava
----

With reference to the <<#defining_composite_builds,example build>>, to execute the `run` task in the `my-app` build from `my-composite`:

[source,bash]
----
$ cd my-composite
$ ./gradlew :my-app:app:run
----

To <<command_line_interface.adoc#sec:excluding_tasks_from_the_command_line,exclude a task from the command line>>, you need to provide the fully qualified path to the task:

[source,bash]
----
$ ./gradlew :my-app:app:compileJava --exclude-task :my-app:app:test
----

You can optionally define a `run` task in `my-composite` that depends on `my-app:app:run`:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/kotlin",files="build.gradle.kts[tags=run]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/groovy",files="build.gradle[tags=run]"]
====

So that you can execute `./gradlew run` from the `my-composite` directory:

[source,bash]
----
$ cd my-composite
$ ./gradlew run
----

NOTE: Included build tasks are automatically executed to generate required dependency artifacts, or the including build can <<#included_build_task_dependencies,declare a dependency on a task>> from an included build.

[[included_build_task_dependencies]]
=== Depending on Tasks

While included builds are isolated from one another and cannot declare direct dependencies, a composite build can declare task dependencies on its included builds.

The included builds are accessed using link:{groovyDslPath}/org.gradle.api.invocation.Gradle.html#org.gradle.api.invocation.Gradle:includedBuilds[Gradle.getIncludedBuilds()] or link:{groovyDslPath}/org.gradle.api.invocation.Gradle.html#org.gradle.api.invocation.Gradle:includedBuild(java.lang.String)[Gradle.includedBuild(java.lang.String)], and a task reference is obtained via the link:{groovyDslPath}/org.gradle.api.initialization.IncludedBuild.html#org.gradle.api.initialization.IncludedBuild:task(java.lang.String)[IncludedBuild.task(java.lang.String)] method.

Using these APIs, it is possible to declare a dependency on a task in a particular included build:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/kotlin",files="build.gradle.kts[tags=run]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/groovy",files="build.gradle[tags=run]"]
====

Or you can declare a dependency on tasks with a certain path in all of the included builds:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-hierarchical-multirepo/kotlin",files="build.gradle.kts"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-hierarchical-multirepo/groovy",files="build.gradle"]
====

[[referencing_included_build_projects]]
=== Referencing Projects

It is a common mistake to attempt to use `project()` notation to depend on a module that resides in an included build.

IMPORTANT: Included builds are not subprojects.

Each build in a composite has its own project hierarchy.
You cannot use project paths (e.g., `project(":other-build:module")`) to reference a project across build boundaries.
Doing so will result in an `UnknownProjectException`.

To depend on a project from an included build, you must use its external coordinates (the same coordinates you would use if the library were published to Maven Central or Ivy).

If an included build has a project with `group = "com.example.data"` and `rootProject.name = "core-schema"`, you reference it in your main build like an external dependency.
For example, if your configuration looks as follows:

====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,kotlin]
----
.
├── app (Composite Build)
│   ├── build.gradle.kts
│   └── settings.gradle.kts  <-- includeBuild("../core-schema")
└── core-schema (Included Build)
    ├── build.gradle.kts
    └── settings.gradle.kts  <-- rootProject.name = "core-schema"
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,groovy]
----
.
├── app (Composite Build)
│   ├── build.gradle
│   └── settings.gradle  <-- includeBuild("../core-schema")
└── core-schema (Included Build)
    ├── build.gradle
    └── settings.gradle  <-- rootProject.name = "core-schema"
----
=====
====

The included build has the following information:

====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,kotlin]
.core-schema/build.gradle.kts
----
group = "com.example.data"
version = "1.0.0"
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,groovy]
.core-schema/build.gradle
----
group = "com.example.data"
version = "1.0.0"
----
=====
====

So that the main build can reference it:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-referencingProjects/kotlin",files="build.gradle.kts[tags=referencing-projects]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-referencingProjects/groovy",files="build.gradle[tags=referencing-projects]"]
====

Gradle uses the metadata from the included build to "discover" which coordinates it provides.
As long as the coordinates match, Gradle replaces the external dependency with a project dependency at execution time, see <<#included_build_declaring_substitutions>> to learn more.

[[composite_build_isolation]]
== Configuring a Composite Build

A critical aspect of included builds is that they are executed in *isolation*.

This has specific implications for how configuration is (or is not) shared:

- *Gradle Properties*: `gradle.properties` files defined in the root build are not visible to included builds. Each included build must define its own properties or properties must be passed via the CLI. +
Note that this applies to user-defined properties. Gradle runtime properties (such as `org.gradle.configuration-cache`) are a special case — they are only read from the *root build* and applied to the entire invocation. Any such properties defined in an included build's `gradle.properties` are ignored.
- *Shared Configuration*: Included builds do not share any configuration with the root build or other included builds. This includes repositories, plugin management, or dependency versions defined in <<sharing_build_logic_between_subprojects.adoc#sec:using_buildsrc,`buildSrc`>> or version catalogs.

Continuing from the example above, where properties are defined in the CLI and in the root `gradle.properties` file:

[source,bash]
----
$ ./gradlew checkAll -PpropertiesMessage="Hello" -DsystemMessage="Hello"
----

The following output is produced, showcasing the propagation of the properties from the root file and the CLI to the included builds:

[source,text]
----
include::{snippetsPath}/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/tests/inheritance.out[]
----

If you need to share credentials (like repository tokens) or common configuration across a composite build tree, consider using system environment variables or extracting the logic into a shared convention plugin included via `pluginManagement`.

While included builds are isolated and cannot declare direct project dependencies, a composite build can <<#included_build_task_dependencies,declare task dependencies>> on its included builds.

[[included_plugin_builds]]
== Gradle Plugins in Composite Builds

When including builds that provide Gradle plugins, there are different approaches depending on how and where the plugin will be applied.

[[including_plugin_builds_in_settings]]
=== Plugins for Build Scripts

Plugins that will be applied in project build scripts (e.g., `build.gradle.kts`) can be included using `includeBuild` in your `settings.gradle(.kts)` file.

This approach is recommended over using the `--include-build` CLI flag, as it provides more reliable plugin resolution, especially when using the modern `plugins {}` block:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/kotlin/my-app",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=mag]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/groovy/my-app",files="settings.gradle[tags=mag]"]
====

Then the plugin is used as follows:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/kotlin",files="my-app/app/build.gradle.kts[tags=plugin_dependencies]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-basic/groovy",files="my-app/app/build.gradle[tags=plugin_dependencies]"]
====

[[including_settings_plugin_builds]]
=== Plugins for Settings Files

A special case of included builds are builds that define plugins that need to be applied in the *settings file itself*.
These builds should be included using the `includeBuild` statement inside the `pluginManagement {}` block of the settings file.

Using this mechanism, the included build may contribute a settings plugin that can be applied in the settings file:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-settingsPlugin/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=settings-plugin]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-settingsPlugin/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=settings-plugin]"]
====

NOTE: While the `--include-build` CLI flag can work for plugins applied via the `buildscript {}` block, it may not work reliably for plugins applied using the modern `plugins {}` block, especially for unpublished plugins.

For consistent behavior, use `includeBuild` in your settings file.
For settings plugins (plugins applied in the settings file itself), use `includeBuild` within the `pluginManagement {}` block.

[[included_build_declaring_substitutions]]
== Dependency Substitution in Composite Builds

By default, Gradle will configure each included build to determine the dependencies it can provide.
The algorithm for doing this is simple.
Gradle will inspect the group and name for the projects in the included build and substitute project dependencies for any external dependency matching `${project.group}:${project.name}`.

[NOTE]
====
By default, substitutions are not registered for the _main_ build.

To make the (sub)projects of the main build addressable by `${project.group}:${project.name}`, you can tell Gradle to treat the main build like an included build by self-including it: `includeBuild(".")`.
====

There are cases when the default substitutions determined by Gradle are insufficient or must be corrected for a particular composite.
For these cases, explicitly declaring the substitutions for an included build is possible.

For example, a single-project build called `anonymous-library`, produces a Java utility library but does not declare a value for the group attribute:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-declared-substitution/kotlin",files="anonymous-library/build.gradle.kts[]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-declared-substitution/groovy",files="anonymous-library/build.gradle[]"]
====

When this build is included in a composite, it will attempt to substitute for the dependency module `undefined:anonymous-library` (`undefined` being the default value for `project.group`, and `anonymous-library` being the root project name).
Clearly, this isn't useful in a composite build.

To use the unpublished library in a composite build, you can explicitly declare the substitutions that it provides:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-declared-substitution/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=composite_substitution]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/composite-builds-declared-substitution/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=composite_substitution]"]
====

With this configuration, the `my-app` composite build will substitute any dependency on `org.sample:number-utils` with a dependency on the root project of `anonymous-library`.

IMPORTANT: Substitutions are not transitive across builds.

Explicitly declared substitutions are only active for the build that defines them.
In the example above, while `my-app` knows to substitute `org.sample:number-utils` with the local `anonymous-library`, the `anonymous-library` build itself remains unaware of this rule.

If you run a task directly from within the `anonymous-library` directory that requires `org.sample:number-utils` (for example, in its own test suite), the resolution will fail unless:

1. The substitution is also declared in the `settings.gradle(.kts)` of `anonymous-library`.
2. (*Recommended*) You align the group and `rootProject.name` of `anonymous-library` to match the expected coordinates, allowing Gradle's default auto-substitution to work in both directions.

[[deactivate_included_build_substitutions]]
=== Disabling Substitutions for a Configuration

If you need to <<declaring_configurations.adoc#sec:resolvable-consumable-configs,resolve>> a published version of a module that is also available as part of an included build, you can deactivate the included build substitution rules on the link:{groovyDslPath}/org.gradle.api.artifacts.ResolutionStrategy.html[`ResolutionStrategy`] of the Configuration that is resolved.
This is necessary because the rules are globally applied in the build, and Gradle does not consider published versions during resolution by default.

For example, we create a separate `publishedRuntimeClasspath` configuration that gets resolved to the published versions of modules that also exist in one of the local builds.
This is done by deactivating global dependency substitution rules:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/customizingResolution-deactivateGlobalSubstitution/kotlin",files="build.gradle.kts[tags=disableGlobalDependencySubstitutionRules]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/customizingResolution-deactivateGlobalSubstitution/groovy",files="build.gradle[tags=disableGlobalDependencySubstitutionRules]"]
====

A use-case would be to compare published and locally built JAR files.

[[included_build_substitution_requirements]]
=== When to Declare Substitutions Explicitly

Many builds will function automatically as an included build, without declared substitutions.
Here are some common cases where declared substitutions are required:

* When the `archivesBaseName` property is used to set the name of the published artifact.
* When a configuration other than `default` is published.
* When the `maven-publish` or `ivy-publish` plugins are used for publishing and the publication coordinates don't match `${project.group}:${project.name}`.
* When multiple publications are defined for a single project (e.g., a project that publishes two different libraries).

[[included_build_substitution_limitations]]
=== When Substitutions Won't Work

Some builds won't function correctly when included in a composite, even when dependency substitutions are explicitly declared.
This limitation is because a substituted project dependency will always point to the `default` configuration of the target project.
Any time the artifacts and dependencies specified for the default configuration of a project don't match what is published to a repository, the composite build may exhibit different behavior.

Here are some cases where the published module metadata may be different from the project default configuration:

* When the `maven-publish` or `ivy-publish` plugins are used with custom logic in the publication block.
* When the `POM` or `ivy.xml` file is tweaked as part of publication.
* When a capability or a custom variant is only defined via publication metadata.

Builds using these features may function incorrectly when included in a composite build.

[[included_builds]]
== Requirements for Composite Builds

Composite builds must maintain unique identifiers for every project across the entire build tree.

To prevent conflicts, Gradle qualifies projects using a build-tree path, which combines the build path (derived from the included build's directory name) and the project path.

To ensure every project remains uniquely addressable, included builds must satisfy two conditions:

1. *Unique Build Paths:* No two included builds can share the same build path.
2. *No Namespace Overlap:* An included build path cannot conflict with any existing project path in the root build.

If directory names cause a naming collision, rename the build path in your settings file:

====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,kotlin]
.settings.gradle.kts
----
includeBuild("some-included-build") {
    name = "other-name"
}
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source,groovy]
.settings.gradle
----
includeBuild('some-included-build') {
    name = 'other-name'
}
----
=====
====

NOTE: When a composite build includes another composite, Gradle flattens the structure. All included builds share the same parent, regardless of how deeply they were nested.

[[current_limitations_and_future_work]]
== Known Limitations of Composite Builds

Limitations of the current implementation include:

* **Substitution Limitations**: No support for included builds with publications that don't mirror the project default configuration.
See <<#included_build_substitution_limitations,Cases where composite builds won't work>>.
* **Multiple Composite Builds**: Multiple composite builds may conflict when run in parallel if more than one includes the same build.
Gradle does not share the project lock of a shared composite build between Gradle invocations to prevent concurrent execution.
* **Configuration-on-Demand**: See <<#composite_build_configuration_on_demand>> below.

[[composite_build_configuration_on_demand]]
=== Configuration-on-Demand

Using <<configuration_on_demand.adoc#configuration_and_execution,Configuration-on-Demand>> with composite builds can significantly impact performance.
The behavior changes depending on whether you rely on default substitutions or explicitly declared substitutions:

1. You must manually declare all dependency substitutions for every project within that included build that you wish to use. Any project not explicitly mapped will be treated as an external dependency.
2. The way Gradle discovers what an included build "provides" dictates how much of that build must be configured at startup:
+
[cols="1,2,2", options="header"]
|===
| Scenario | Behavior | Performance Impact

| **Default Rules** (No explicit substitutions)
| Gradle must inspect every project in the included build to find matching `group` and `name`.
| *High:* The included build is **always fully configured**, even if its projects aren't needed for the current task.

| **Explicit Rules** (Using `substitute...`)
| Gradle uses your explicit rules as the source of truth.
| *Optimized:* The included build is **not configured** unless a task requires one of the substituted projects.
|===


<a id="doc-5cc40eb4e23f1617e1e1ebcc"></a>

[[configuration_and_execution]]
= Configuration On Demand

Configuration-on-demand attempts to configure only the relevant projects for the requested tasks, i.e., it only evaluates the build script file of projects participating in the build.
This way, the configuration time of a large multi-project build can be reduced.

The configuration-on-demand feature is _incubating_, so only some builds are guaranteed to work correctly.
The feature works well for <<#sec:decoupled_projects,decoupled>> multi-project builds.

In configuration-on-demand mode, projects are configured as follows:

* The root project is always configured.
* The project in the directory where the build is executed is also configured, but only when Gradle is executed without any tasks. +
This way, the default tasks behave correctly when projects are configured on demand.
* The standard project dependencies are supported, and relevant projects are configured. +
If project A has a compile dependency on project B, then building A causes the configuration of both projects.
* The task dependencies declared via the task path are supported and cause relevant projects to be configured. +
Example: `someTask.dependsOn(":some-other-project:someOtherTask")`
* A task requested via task path from the command line (or tooling API) causes the relevant project to be configured. +
For example, building `project-a:project-b:someTask` causes configuration of `project-b`.

[[sec:configuration_on_demand]]
== Enable `configure-on-demand`

You can enable configuration-on-demand using the `--configure-on-demand` flag or adding `org.gradle.configureondemand=true` to the `gradle.properties` file.

To configure on demand with every build run, see <<build_environment.adoc#sec:gradle_configuration_properties,Gradle properties>>.

To configure on demand for a given build, see <<command_line_interface.adoc#sec:command_line_performance,command-line performance-oriented options>>.

[[sec:decoupled_projects]]
== Decoupled projects

Gradle allows projects to access each other's configurations and tasks during the configuration and execution phases.
While this flexibility empowers build authors, it limits Gradle's ability to perform optimizations such as <<#sec:parallel_execution,parallel project builds>> and <<#configuration_and_execution,configuration on demand>>.

Projects are considered decoupled when they interact solely through declared dependencies and task dependencies.
Any direct modification or reading of another project's object creates coupling between the projects.
Coupling during configuration can result in flawed build outcomes when using 'configuration on demand', while coupling during execution can affect parallel execution.

One common source of coupling is configuration injection, such as using `allprojects{}` or `subprojects{}` in build scripts.

To avoid coupling issues, it's recommended to:

- Refrain from referencing other subprojects' build scripts and prefer cross-project configuration from the root project.
- Avoid dynamically changing other projects' configurations during execution.

As Gradle evolves, it aims to provide features that leverage decoupled projects while offering solutions for common use cases like configuration injection without introducing coupling.

[[sec:parallel_execution]]
== Parallel projects

Gradle's parallel execution feature optimizes CPU utilization to accelerate builds by concurrently executing tasks from different projects.

To enable parallel execution, use the `--parallel` <<command_line_interface.adoc#sec:command_line_performance,command-line argument>> or configure your <<build_environment.adoc#sec:gradle_configuration_properties,build environment>>.
Gradle automatically determines the optimal number of parallel threads based on CPU cores.

During parallel execution, each worker handles a specific project exclusively.
Task dependencies are respected, with workers prioritizing upstream tasks.
However, tasks may not execute in alphabetical order, as in sequential mode.
It's crucial to correctly declare task dependencies and inputs/outputs to avoid ordering issues.

[[multi_project_builds]]
= Multi-Project Builds
:keywords: multi, project, subprojects, multi-project

As projects grow, it's common to split them into smaller, focused modules that are built, tested, and released together.
Gradle supports this through multi-project builds, allowing you to organize related codebases under a single build while keeping each module logically isolated.

[[multi_project_layout]]
== Multi-Project Layout

A multi-project build consists of a root project and one or more subprojects, all defined in a single `settings.gradle(.kts)` file.
This structure supports modularization, parallel execution, and code reuse.

image::structuring-builds-6.png[]

A typical multi-project structure looks like this:

[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, kotlin]
----
my-project/
├── settings.gradle.kts     // <1>
├── build.gradle.kts            // <2>
├── app/                    // <3>
│   └── build.gradle.kts        // <4>
├── core/                   // <3>
│   └── build.gradle.kts        // <5>
└── util/                   // <3>
    └── build.gradle.kts        // <6>
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, groovy]
----
my-project/
├── settings.gradle         // <1>
├── build.gradle        // <2>
├── app/                    // <3>
│   └── build.gradle    // <4>
├── core/                   // <3>
│   └── build.gradle    // <5>
└── util/                   // <3>
    └── build.gradle    // <6>
----
=====
<1> Declares subprojects
<2> Root project build logic (optional)
<3> Subproject
<4> App module
<5> Shared core logic
<6> Utility code

Each subproject can define its own build logic, dependencies, and plugins.

In `settings.gradle(.kts)`, you include subprojects by name using `include()`.
The `include()` method takes <<multi_project_builds_intermediate.adoc#sec:project_path,project paths>> as arguments:

[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, kotlin]
----
rootProject.name = "my-project"
include("app", "core", "util")
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, groovy]
----
rootProject.name = 'my-project'
include('app', 'core', 'util')
----
=====

By default, a project path corresponds to the relative physical location of the project directory.
For example, the path `services:api` maps to the directory `./services/api`, relative to the root project.

You can find more examples and detailed usage in the DSL reference for link:{groovyDslPath}++/org.gradle.api.initialization.Settings.html#org.gradle.api.initialization.Settings:include(java.lang.String[])++[`Settings.include(String...)`].

[[sub:modifying_element_of_the_project_tree]]
=== Project Descriptors

To further describe the project architecture to Gradle, the settings file provides _project descriptors_.

You can modify these descriptors in the settings file at any time.

To access a descriptor, you can:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/customLayout/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=lookup-project]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/customLayout/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=lookup-project]"]
====

Using this descriptor, you can change the name, project directory, and build file of a project:

====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/customLayout/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[tags=change-project]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/customLayout/groovy",files="settings.gradle[tags=change-project]"]
====

Consult the link:{javadocPath}/org/gradle/api/initialization/ProjectDescriptor.html[ProjectDescriptor] class in the API documentation for more information.

NOTE: Setting the link:{groovyDslPath}/org.gradle.api.Project.html#org.gradle.api.Project:projectDir[Project.projectDir] property is important when locating projects in nested subdirectories to <<best_practices_structuring_builds.adoc#avoid_empty_projects,avoid unintentionally creating empty projects>>.

[[include_existing_projects_only]]
=== Including projects without an existing directory

When you include a subproject in your `settings.gradle(.kts)` file, Gradle expects that the associated directory for that project exists and is writable.

WARNING: Starting with **Gradle 9.0.0**, this is enforced strictly: **If a project directory is missing or read-only, the build will fail.** This replaces earlier behavior where Gradle would silently allow missing project directories.

Here's how you can create a missing directory at configuration time:

=====
[.multi-language-sample]
======
.settings.gradle.kts
[source,kotlin]
----
include("project-without-directory")
project(":project-without-directory").projectDir.mkdirs()
----
======
[.multi-language-sample]
======
.settings.gradle
[source,groovy]
----
include 'project-without-directory'
project(":project-without-directory").projectDir.mkdirs()
----
======
=====

[[sec:naming_recommendations]]
== Naming recommendations

As your project grows, naming and consistency get increasingly more important.

To keep your builds maintainable, we recommend the following:

1. *Keep default project names for subprojects*:
It is possible to configure custom project names in the settings file.
However, it’s an unnecessary extra effort for the developers to track which projects belong to what folders.

2. *Use lower case hyphenation for all project names*:
All letters are lowercase, and words are separated with a dash (`-`) character.

3. *Define the root project name in the settings file*:
The `rootProject.name` effectively assigns a name to the build, used in reports like Build Scan.
If the root project name is not set, the name will be the container directory name, which can be unstable (i.e., you can check out your project in any directory).
The name will be generated randomly if the root project name is not set and checked out to a file system's root (e.g., `/` or `C:\`).

[[declaring_dependencies_between_subprojects]]
== Declaring dependencies between Subprojects

What if one subproject depends on another?
What if one subproject depends on the artifact produced by another?

image::structuring-builds-7.png[]

This is a common use case in multi-project builds.
Gradle supports this scenario with <<declaring_dependencies_basics.adoc#sec:project-dependencies,project dependencies>>.

[[sec:project_jar_dependencies]]
=== Depending on another Project

Consider a multi-project build with the following layout:

[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, kotlin]
----
.
├── api
│   ├── src
│   │   └──...
│   └── build.gradle.kts
├── services
│   └── person-service
│       ├── src
│       │   └──...
│       └── build.gradle.kts
├── shared
│   ├── src
│   │   └──...
│   └── build.gradle.kts
└── settings.gradle.kts
----
=====
[.multi-language-sample]
=====
[source, groovy]
----
.
├── api
│   ├── src
│   │   └──...
│   └── build.gradle
├── services
│   └── person-service
│       ├── src
│       │   └──...
│       └── build.gradle
├── shared
│   ├── src
│   │   └──...
│   └── build.gradle
└── settings.gradle
----
=====

In this example:

1. `person-service` depends on both `api` and `shared`
2. `api` depends on `shared`

You declare these relationships using the project path, which uses colons (`:`) to indicate nesting.
For example:

- `:shared` refers to the `shared` subproject
- `services:person-service` refers to a nested subproject

[[javadependencies_2]]
====
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/basic-dependencies/kotlin",files="settings.gradle.kts[];shared/build.gradle.kts[];api/build.gradle.kts[];services/person-service/build.gradle.kts[]"]
include::sample[dir="snippets/structuring-builds/basic-dependencies/groovy",files="settings.gradle[];shared/build.gradle[];api/build.gradle[];services/person-service/build.gradle[]"]
====

For more details on project paths, consult the DSL documentation for link:{groovyDslPath}++/org.gradle.api.initialization.Settings.html#org.gradle.api.initialization.Settings:include(java.lang.String[])++[Settings.include(String...)].

A project dependency affects both the build order and classpath:

- The required project will be built first.
- Its compiled classes and transitive dependencies are added to the consuming project’s classpath.

For example, running `./gradlew :api:compileJava` will first build `shared`, then `api`.

[[sec:depending_on_output_of_another_project]]
=== Depending on Artifacts produced by another Project

Sometimes, you only need the output of a specific task from another project—not the entire project itself.

While you can create task-to-task dependencies between projects, Gradle discourages this because it creates tight coupling between tasks.

Instead, use outgoing artifacts to expose a task’s output and model it as a dependency.
Gradle’s <<variant_aware_resolution.adoc#sec:understanding-variant-selection,variant-aware dependency management>> allows one project to consume artifacts from another in a structured, on-demand way.
